nodes.title: TAXONOMY
nodes.body:
Common Name:  Striped mojarra
Scientific Name: Eugerres plumieri

nodes.title: Classification
nodes.body:
Phylum:  Chordata
	Class:  Actinopterygii
	Order:  Perciformes
	Family:  Gerreidae

Other Common Names:  sand perch, goat, sand brim (664).
Note: Diapterus plumieri - invalid - subsequent name/combination

nodes.title: VALUE & STATUS
nodes.body:
Commercial:  Occasionally sold in markets in the Tampa Bay area (664).  Commonly seen in some of the smaller fish markets (1036).  Diapterus plumieri is captured with D. auratus in Indian River Lagoon commercial mojarra fishery (1272).  This fishery has undoubtedly been lumped with the "sand perch" category in Florida's commercial landings reports (e.g.  1162)

Recreational:  Occasional landings are reported in the recreational fishery (848).

Indicator: Has been used in eye research (e.g. Plaza-Yglesias et al. 1988).

nodes.title: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
nodes.body:
Overall:  From South Carolina, throughout the Gulf of Mexico to Brazil.  Absent in the Bahamas and smaller islands of the West Indies (788).

Within Study Area:  Found in Florida waters from approximately 28 N latitude south (664 848  887 1272).  Found in the IRL system generally associated with freshwater tributaries and estuarine wetlands (848 887 1272).  Not collected by Snelson in the northern portion of the lagoon (1242).

Mobility and Migration:

nodes.title: Life Mode
nodes.body: Generally a schooling species (664), which usually occurs at or near the bottom (790).  Euryhaline, benthic feeder associated with freshwater tributaries and estuarine wetlands (848 702 1105 1204).

nodes.title: BENTHIC HABITAT
nodes.body:
Habitat Type: Found in brackish and coastal freshwaters (788).  Occurs in most coastal rivers and some canals many kilometers from saltwater (790).  Not found to any great extent in seagrass beds of the IRL (993) but generally associated with freshwater tributaries and estuarine wetlands (848 1272).

Substrate:  Associated with partially submerged rocks in the Tampa Bay area (664), and also found in grassy areas (788).  Appears to be associated with softer bottoms in the IRL (1272).

nodes.title: Eggs/Larvae
nodes.body: Juvenile/adults:  Collected in Tampa Bay at temperatures from 21.1 to 32.5 65 C (664) and the IRL around Jupiter from 21.0 to 36 C (887).  Springer and Woodburn (664) found them dead at temperatures of around 13 C in Tampa Bay, while Gilmore et al. found them dead in the IRL at between 6-9 C (236).

nodes.title: Eggs/Larvae
nodes.body: Juvenile/adults:  Collected at salinities of 3.7 to 24.8 ppt in Tampa Bay (664).  Especially abundant in the Peace River at salinities from 0 to 5.4 ppt (789).  Reported from freshwater (0 ppt) in the St. Lucie River (664) and from 1.5 to 34.9 ppt in the Jupiter Inlet area (887).  Collected in the southern IRL and its tributaries in salinities from 0 to 38.5 ppt (1271).  Also reported as the common freshwater mojarra in the Everglades (790).  All reports of occurrences in freshwater are from Florida (1037).

nodes.title: REPRODUCTION
nodes.body:
Reproductive Mode:  Reproduction is sexual with external fertilization.

Mating/Spawning: In Florida, spawning has been reported to occur in freshwater (Robins cited in (790)).

Fecundity: In hormone induced spawning experiments, females between 14 and 19 cm TL produce from 18,025 to 68,380 eggs (mean of 43,823; Millares et al. 1979)

nodes.title: Length Range
nodes.body:
Eggs:  Planktonic (Matheson pers. comm.).  In hormone induced spawning experiments, eggs were spherical and translucent with one oil droplet.  The mean diameter of the eggs and the droplet were 584 +/- 3mm and 159 +/- 2 mm, respectively.  Hatching took place in most case at around 24 h at average temperatures of 25 and 28 C (Millares et al. 1979).

 Larvae:  Planktonic (Matheson pers. comm.).  Recently hatched larvae obtained by Borrero and Millares (1979) by induced spawning had a mean length of 1.370 mm.  Mean yolk sac and oil droplet diameters were 0.512 and 0.165 mm, respectively.  Absorption of the yolk sac and oil droplet was complete in 31 h and 96 h, respectively, at 28 C, while it took 53 h and 122 h at 24 C.  Larvae that were not fed died in 104 h at 28 C and 149 h at 24 C.  Metamorphosis was complete between 30 and 35 days at approximately 10 mm TL (Borrero and Millares 1979)
Juveniles:  In the laboratory, the juvenile stage was reached in approximately one month at 10 mm TL (Borrero and Millares 1979).
Adults:  Maximum size reported as 30 cm (788).  Have been collected to 250 mm SL in the IRL (1271)

nodes.title: FOOD HABITS
nodes.body: Reported to probe the substrate for food items (790).  Adults known to feed on benthic and epibenthic ostracods, mysids, amphipods, and polychaetes, while juveniles may also prey on copepods (279 664 1204).

nodes.body: Richard E. Matheson; Florida Marine Research Institute, Dept. of Environmental Protection, St. Petersburg, Florida
